author: Keshav S.
text:
Unpopular opinion: most companies are hiring the wrong people for AI.
They post a job for a "Machine Learning Engineer," wait 4 months, pay a fortune, and finally hire one person.

Then that one person is expected to:
 → Build the data pipeline
 → Train the model
 → Deploy it to the cloud
 → Set up monitoring & retraining
 → And somehow maintain it all

That's not one job. That's four. And it's why so many AI projects stall — you can't ship production AI with a single overloaded hire.
Production AI is a team sport: ML + DevOps + backend, working together. That's the part nobody tells you before the budget's already spent.
It's also exactly why we work the way we do — a full AI/ML team that takes your idea to a live, production system end-to-end. Fixed scope. Fixed price. Shipped, not stuck in a notebook.
If your AI roadmap is bottlenecked on "we need to hire someone first" — that's the assumption worth questioning.

Building AI in-house or bringing in a team — what's working for you? 👇

author: Aidan O'Toole
text:
Recently moving from the UK to Melbourne and recruiting across Australia's Data & AI market, one thing has become clear: demand isn't slowing down, it's evolving.

I've been speaking with Data Engineers, Data Scientists, AI Engineers, ML Engineers, Analytics professionals and hiring leaders across Australia.

A few trends I'm consistently seeing:
• More organisations moving beyond AI experimentation and focusing on deploying solutions into production. 
• Growing demand for AI Engineering and MLOps capability as businesses look to scale AI initiatives effectively.
• Increasing demand for professionals who can combine strong data foundations with practical AI delivery.
• Continued investment in modern data platforms such as Databricks, Snowflake, Microsoft Fabric and cloud-native technologies. 

One report that caught my attention recently was Deloitte's State of AI in the Enterprise, which found that while Australian organisations continue to invest in AI, many are still working through the challenge of moving projects from pilot stages into production at scale.

For me, that's where some of the most interesting hiring activity is taking place.
The conversation is increasingly shifting away from:
"How do we experiment with AI?"
Towards:
"How do we operationalise it, govern it, and create meaningful business outcomes?" 

As someone who has recently entered the Australian market, it's been fascinating to learn from candidates, hiring managers and technology leaders across the space.

I'd be interested to hear your perspective:

author: D Vishesh R.
text:
I joined an interview in 2026, but felt like I time-traveled to 2019.

I just had one of the most surreal #interviews ever.

The recruiter—3rd party contractor for a #WITCH company—kept their cameras off, asking me to rotate mine to exhibit my bedroom, with no regard of my #privacy.

And the questions?
Textbook trivia from 2019: Bagging, Stacking, basic Python puzzle

0 questions about building observable, reliable & evaluative systems.
0 curiosity about production-grade #RAG pipelines, multi-agent orchestration or the local-first containerized deployments that I actually built. 

When the spotlight kept hitting irrelevant trivia, I froze. 
I forgot what ensemble-learning was, as my brain short-circuited by the gas-lighting.

But here is the reality-check that hit me afterward:

While I was prepping for a process, designed to evaluate nothing except my ability to survive a hazing ritual. 
The AI world just witnessed #KimiK3 slash a million-token context window cost by ~1/2. 
Researchers just published techniques cutting token usage by 40%. 

The industry is racing toward hyper-efficiency, local-first agents & cost-optimized inference.

To keep up with it this what  I think WITCH companies need to do, but won't (because bureaucracy):
Assignment-based hiring.

Give me a real problem. Give me 48 hours. 
Let me build something. 
Let me show you how I think, how I debug, how I ship.

Instead, we get:
- Memorisation-test of questions irrelevant to the JD
- Interviewers threatened by up-to-speed candidates
- 3rd-party recruiters who treat talent like cattle

If India's massive service giants continue hiring AI/ML talents based on legacy trivia, rather than 2026 engineering reality, they are aligning themselves up for a brutal wake-up call. 

The #GenAI #bubble is unironically thinning.
Post-bubble businesses won't pay for legacy trivia-memorisers, but for engineers who can ship observable, reliant & evaluative solutions.
I have already written about this earlier.

To every AI/ML #candidate out there:
Don't lower your expectations. 

If you're an AI/ML engineer who builds production systems, don't be disheartened by some trivia-memorising fidelity-test.

Vet the process before you invest your time & energy.
Aim for Startups & Mid-tier companies.
Especially emphasize industries that touch 'atoms' instead of 'bits'. 

The 3rd-party recruiters are often disconnected from the actual work. 
They're gate-keepers who don't understand the gate. 
Be skeptical. Protect your time.

And if you ever wonder the lack of India-first Foundational AI development by any of these Tech giants, do remember that these companies are not incentivised for #innovation but for virtue-arbitrage.

Do share if you've had similar experiences!

text:
Here's a number that should reframe how every company plans its AI team in India. Industry estimates put India's AI and ML skills deficit at roughly 53 percent right now. For every two AI roles a GCC posts, less than one qualified candidate is actually available. 

That's not a reason to slow down. It's a reason to change how you engage.

The old approach, post a generic "AI Engineer" job description and wait for resumes to arrive, was already broken for regular tech roles. For AI specifically, it doesn't work at all. The companies actually closing this gap are doing two things differently. They're hiring against specific skill clusters, GenAI, MLOps, applied ML, rather than vague titles. And they're using a build, operate, transfer model instead of trying to run a from-scratch search themselves, which the data shows compresses time-to-operations by 30 to 40 percent compared to a DIY setup.

The honest version of the timeline conversation isn't "we can get you an AI team in a few weeks no matter what." It's "the gap is real, but the way you search for talent determines whether you're waiting months longer than you need to."

We'd rather tell founders the real number than a comfortable one.

What's been the hardest part of building an AI team in India for you, finding the capability, or figuring out what to actually acquire the capability for?

author: Gowtham M
text:
The AI hiring market is not broken because there are too few jobs.
It is broken because too many “AI Engineer” jobs do not tell you what they actually want.

I went through 12,286 live AI/ML engineering job postings from LinkedIn this month.

Not career advice.
Not a “top 10 AI skills” thread.
The actual descriptions companies have put out.
And honestly, it made me feel bad for people trying to break in.

A job titled AI Engineer sounds broad enough for a capable builder to apply.
Then you open it.
Python. ML. LLMs. RAG. Agents. LangChain or LangGraph. MCP. Docker. Kubernetes. Cloud. CI/CD. Data pipelines. Evaluation. Sometimes research publications too.

That is not one role.

That is a small AI team compressed into one job description.
The title is often hiding the real ask:
- Only 3% of postings mention “agentic” in the title
But 65% of generic “AI Engineer” postings ask for agentic-AI skills in the description
- 62% of titles do not say “senior,” yet the roles that state experience requirements commonly ask for around five years
The average posting spans 4.6 technical cat!

So if you are wondering why your résumé feels like it is becoming outdated every few months: you are not imagining it.
The job changed.
The title stayed the same.
And here is the part that hurts.
Everyone says: “Learn the new stuff early and you’ll stand out.”
But the “new stuff” already has a queue.

LangGraph-related roles show a median of 910 applicants.
Fine-tuning: 816.
Agentic AI: 762.
MCP: 703.

The research/publication-heavy lane is lower, at 46.

So no-watching one LangGraph tutorial is not a moat.
Neither is adding “AI agents” to your LinkedIn headline.
The market is crowded with people learning the same visible skills at the same time.

There is another uncomfortable reality candidates keep talking about privately:
Some applications are filtered before a recruiter ever evaluates your work-location, work authorization, sponsorship, notice period, salary range, profile completeness, keyword matching, or simply the volume of applicants. And for smaller companies without a full recruiting stack, the process can be painfully manual.

That does not mean every open role is fake.
But it does mean an “Easy Apply” submission is not the same thing as being considered.

My biggest takeaway from this research:
- Stop optimising only for the title.
- Stop assuming “AI Engineer” means entry level.
- Stop treating every public job post as an equally real opportunity.
- Read the description like an investigator.
- Look for the actual product problem.
- Check whether the company has a real engineering team.
- Find the hiring manager or technical lead.
- Build proof that maps to their stack.
Because right now, the AI job market is not rewarding people who collect the most buzzwords.

text:
Here's the mechanism behind that number. It's not that AI wiped out entry-level hiring in India, it split it in two.

HCLTech has said around 15 percent of its fresher hiring now goes to specialised, AI-related roles. TCS, HCLTech, Infosys and Wipro are all building out a distinct, elite cadre of fresher recruits with advanced AI skills, some call them Forward Deployed Engineers. Meanwhile, across the board, 60 to 70 percent of fresher job descriptions now list AI or ML proficiency as a core requirement, even in roles that have nothing to do with AI on paper. Freshers who can actually demonstrate those skills are commanding a 25 to 40 percent premium over classical IT hires.

That's why the campus placement numbers look so grim in aggregate. Two different job markets are hiding inside one placement season, and most final-year students are still being prepared for the one that's shrinking, not the one that's paying a premium.

I mentor a fair number of people walking into exactly this fork. The gap almost never comes down to raw ability. It comes down to whether anyone told them the fork existed.
